newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia '96 trade deficit forecast revised down.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia '96 trade deficit forecast revised down.

text.p: Malaysia's 1996 trade deficit forecast has been revised downward to an average 4.95 billion ringgit from 8.55 billion three months ago, according to a Reuter poll of economists on Wednesday.
This compared with a trade gap of 9.2 billion ringgit last year.

The economists said the revision follows a sharply lower trade deficit of 798.4 million ringgit in the first six months of the current year against a 5.6 billion gap in the corresponding period of last year.
The results are an average of a poll of nine large research houses of the region. The predictions ranged from a deficit of seven billion ringgit to a surplus of 400 million.
The earlier poll in June included 18 economists from various research houses.

The economists also varied in their reasons for the sharp improvement in the trade balance. Among the main reasons suggested was a drop in electronics exports in the second half, higher imports of large one-time equipment and machinery, drop in value of commodity exports and the ringgit's appreciation against the yen.

They said while the recent rise of ringgit against yen has improved the trade balance in the first half, the one time machinery imports, drop in commodity prices and electronics export slump will add to the deficit in the second half.

"First commodity export values came down. Couple that with electronics exports which will come down and the lumpy imports expected, they will increase the import number (and widen deficit in the second half)," said Patrick Er, economist with CIMB Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
"Going by the current trend (of the first half) trade deficit should be two billion ringgit, which is too dramatic an improvement," said Andy Tan, economist with MMS International in Singapore.
"The trade deficit will most certainly improve over the last year, but it will not be that dramatic. It should be around five billion ringgit," he said.
He said the rise of the trade deficit in the second half was probably because large imports such as aircraft, ships and trains had not been completed yet.
